chapter_summary:
Actuators are the output devices that let a Raspberry Pi move or control things in the physical world. The three most common types are servos, DC motors, and relays.

A servo motor can be positioned at a specific angle. Standard hobby servos can move from 0 to 180 degrees. They have three wires: power, ground, and signal. The signal wire connects to a GPIO pin capable of PWM. `gpiozero` provides a `Servo` class:

```python
from gpiozero import Servo
from time import sleep

servo = Servo(17)

servo.min()
sleep(1)
servo.mid()
sleep(1)
servo.max()
sleep(1)
servo.detach()
```

Some servos are continuous rotation servos, which rotate like DC motors rather than moving to a fixed angle. They are useful for small robots and wheels.

DC motors spin continuously when power is applied. They draw more current than a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin can supply, so you cannot connect them directly. Instead, use a motor driver module such as the L298N or L293D. These modules allow you to control motor speed with PWM and direction with additional logic pins. The `gpiozero` `Motor` class simplifies control:

```python
from gpiozero import Motor
from time import sleep

motor = Motor(forward=17, backward=18)

motor.forward(speed=0.5)
sleep(2)
motor.stop()
```

The motor driver's power supply must be separate from the Raspberry Pi's 5V pin for larger motors. Always connect the grounds of the two power supplies together so they share a common reference.

A relay is an electrically operated switch. It lets a Raspberry Pi control high-voltage devices such as lamps, fans, or pumps using a low-voltage signal. Relay modules designed for microcontrollers usually include an optocoupler and a flyback diode to protect the Pi. You can control a relay with the `gpiozero` `OutputDevice` class:

```python
from gpiozero import OutputDevice
from time import sleep

pump = OutputDevice(20)

pump.on()
sleep(5)
pump.off()
```

Never work with mains voltage unless you have proper training and safety equipment. Even low-voltage projects with relays should be double-checked for loose wires and exposed conductors.

screens.title: Motors, Relays, and Actuators
screens.subtitle: Move the physical world: servos, DC motors, motor drivers, and relays for safe switching

narration.text: Actuators are the parts of your Raspberry Pi project that turn code into motion and control. In this lesson you will learn how servo motors let you set a precise angle, how DC motors provide continuous rotation when driven by a motor driver, and how relays let the Pi switch higher-voltage devices safely. We will also cover the important wiring pattern of using an external power supply for motors and tying grounds together so the Pi and the driver share a reference. Concrete examples include sweeping a servo to point a sensor, spinning a motor forward and reverse at different speeds for a small robot, and using a relay module to toggle a lamp while keeping the Pi safe. You will see small code examples using gpiozero that demonstrate the exact classes you will run: Servo, Motor, and OutputDevice. Throughout, I’ll call out common mistakes — like powering a motor directly from a GPIO pin — and practical safety checks you can do before applying power. By the end you’ll understand which actuator to choose, how to wire it, and how to control it reliably and safely.

keyIdea.title: Chapter focus
keyIdea.text: Learn to control servos, drive DC motors via motor drivers, switch devices with relays, and wire external power safely using gpiozero.

Motors, Relays, and Actuators

Turn code into movement. Learn how to position a servo, spin a DC motor with a driver, and switch mains safely with a relay.

DC motors & drivers
Use a motor driver and separate power supply to control speed and direction.
Relays & safety

Coming up: wiring checks, sample code, common mistakes, and a hands-on activity to sweep a servo and toggle a relay.

How servo, motor driver, and relay connect to the Pi and power.

Relay module

Actuators convert electrical signals into motion. Always use proper drivers and separate power for motors, and respect safety when switching mains with relays.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (Detailed)
screens.subtitle: What success looks like and quick verification steps

narration.text: These expanded objectives explain how you'll verify success. For the servo objective, you will run a small script that moves to min, mid, and max positions and observe the arm sweep smoothly without jitter; that shows correct wiring and PWM timing. For DC motors, success is a driver-powered motor that moves forward, stops, and reverses at controlled speeds without dropping the Pi's power or resetting. For relays, success is toggling a test lamp or low-voltage motor while the Pi stays powered and the relay module shows a clear click or state change; you must always confirm insulation and secure terminals first. For external power, success means you used a separate motor supply sized for the motor, tied the grounds together, and confirmed that applying motor power does not alter Pi GPIO logic levels. Each objective includes a short check you can run and a clear sign that wiring and power are correct. These verification steps reduce chance of damage and increase confidence before you move to more complex robotics or mains-controlled projects.

screens.title: What is an actuator?
screens.subtitle: How actuators convert electrical signals into motion or switching action

narration.text: An actuator is any device that converts an electrical signal into physical action. In Raspberry Pi projects actuators are the output hardware you control to move parts or switch circuits: servos set an angle, DC motors spin continuously, and relays act as electrically controlled switches. Understanding this definition helps you pick the right device: use a servo when you need precise angular control, a DC motor for continuous rotation and torque, and a relay when you must switch a separate higher-voltage circuit. A common misconception is treating a GPIO pin like a power source for a motor; GPIO lines provide tiny amounts of current for logic, not motor torque. Instead, actuators often require external power supplies and interface circuitry such as motor drivers or relay modules. For example, a servo typically has three wires — power, ground, and a PWM signal — and expects that the PWM pin reference matches the motor supply ground. The core practical insight is that actuators need the right interface: the Pi provides control signals, and external hardware provides the power and protection required for safe movement and switching. When you design a circuit, name the actuator, identify its supply needs, and choose the driver or relay that matches those needs.

keyIdea.title: Actuator definition
keyIdea.text: Actuators turn electrical signals into motion or switching. Choose a device by whether you need angle, continuous rotation, or safe switching of a separate circuit.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is an actuator?
Definition

An actuator converts electrical signals into physical motion or switching. Examples used here are servos, DC motors, and relays.

Servo
Precise angle control, usually 0–180 degrees, requires PWM signal and power.
DC motor
Continuous rotation and speed control using a motor driver and PWM for speed.
Relay
An electrically operated switch for controlling higher-voltage loads from a low-voltage signal.
Key Takeaway

Pick the actuator that matches motion type and power needs, and always plan an interface that supplies motor power separately from the Pi's logic pins.

Concrete example
A small pan-tilt camera: servos control angles for pan and tilt while a relay could switch a separate camera heater on and off. The Pi sends PWM to the servos and toggles the relay with a safe low-voltage signal.
Common misconception
Never assume a GPIO can supply motor current. GPIO provides a control signal only; motors require separate power and often a driver with protection.
Try this
Identify an actuator in a project and list its power and signal pins. Decide if you need a driver or relay to interface it with the Pi.

screens.title: Servo motors: wires, ranges, and PWM
screens.subtitle: Understand the three-wire servo and what each connection does

narration.text: Most hobby servos have three wires: power, ground, and a signal line that carries a PWM control. The power wire supplies the servo's internal motor and electronics; typical small servos use 5 volts but always check the device rating. Ground must be shared with the Raspberry Pi so the signal reference is correct. The signal line connects to a GPIO pin capable of PWM so the servo interprets the pulse positions. Standard hobby servos move to an angular range such as 0 to 180 degrees when you send the corresponding PWM commands. A common process for wiring a servo is: first, identify the three wires and the power rating; second, connect the servo's ground and the Pi ground together; third, connect the servo power to a suitable supply; fourth, connect the signal wire to a PWM-capable GPIO pin; finally, test with a short script that moves to min, mid, and max positions. A common mistake is powering the servo from the Pi's 5V pin when the servo draws more current than the Pi can provide; use a separate supply when needed. This wiring process ensures the servo receives stable power while the Pi provides the correct signal timing.

keyIdea.title: Servo wiring process
keyIdea.text: Always identify power/ground/signal, share ground with the Pi, power the servo from an appropriate supply, and use a PWM-capable GPIO for the signal.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Servo motors: wires, ranges, and PWM
Three-wire servo
Power
Provides motor current; often 5V for hobby servos. Use a supply sized for the servo's stall current.
Ground
Common reference. Tie servo ground to the Pi ground so the signal has the correct reference voltage.
Signal
PWM pulses from a GPIO pin tell the servo what angle to hold. Use gpiozero's Servo class for control.
Concrete wiring example
Connect servo power to a 5V supply capable of the servo's current, tie grounds together, and attach the signal wire to GPIO 17 if it supports PWM on your Pi model. After wiring, run a short sweep script to confirm movement.
Common mistake
Using the Pi's 5V pin for high-current servos can cause browning out or damage. If the servo draws significant current, use a dedicated supply and test at low load first.
Try this
Label the three servo wires on a real model and trace where each connects in your circuit. Confirm your supplies and common ground before powering up.

screens.title: Positioning a servo with gpiozero
screens.subtitle: See a short script that sweeps a servo between min, mid, and max

narration.text: Controlling a servo from Python is straightforward with gpiozero's Servo class. The typical script creates a Servo instance attached to a GPIO pin, then calls methods to move it to preset positions such as minimum, middle, and maximum. Running these positions with short pauses lets you verify the motion range and wiring. The code example shown uses methods named min, mid, max, and detach to release control after the moves. A practical tip is to always test with small movements first to ensure the servo is not hitting mechanical stops that draw excessive current. A common misconception is that a single command will be instantaneous; in reality the servo moves at its own speed, so scripts usually include short pauses between commands to let the servo reach the position. In practice you will connect the signal to a PWM-capable pin and power the servo from a supply sized for its current. After the sweep, detaching the servo is useful when you want to avoid holding current in the servo while the system is idle. Try running the sweep and watching for smooth motion and consistent endpoints.

keyIdea.title: Servo control via gpiozero
keyIdea.text: Use Servo(min/mid/max/detach) to sweep and validate servo range; pause between commands so the motor reaches each position.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Positioning a servo with gpiozero
Code example
from gpiozero import Servo
from time import sleep

servo = Servo(17)

servo.min()
sleep(1)
servo.mid()
sleep(1)
servo.max()
sleep(1)
servo.detach()
This sequence moves to min, mid, and max with pauses to let the servo reach each position, then detaches to stop holding current.
Explanation
  • Create a Servo bound to a GPIO pin that supports PWM.
  • Call min, mid, and max to move the horn; include sleep so movement completes.
  • Detach to let the servo stop holding position and reduce current draw.
  • Use a separate power supply if the servo draws more current than the Pi can safely deliver.
Common mistake

Not allowing time between commands can yield abrupt movement or incomplete travel. Pause so the servo reaches each target.

screens.title: Standard vs continuous-rotation servos
screens.subtitle: When to use position control and when you need continuous rotation

narration.text: Standard hobby servos are designed for positional control: you request an angle and the servo holds that position. Continuous-rotation servos are modified or designed to rotate continuously like DC motors; the control input maps to rotation speed and direction rather than a target angle. Choose a standard servo when you need precise angular placement such as steering a camera or a control surface. Choose a continuous-rotation servo when you need wheel motion for small robots or continuous turning without positional feedback. An important contrast is how you interpret the control signal: for a normal servo, the signal sets a desired angle; for a continuous servo, the same signal maps to speed and direction. A common misconception is assuming a continuous-rotation servo can hold a fixed angle — it cannot, unless you add external feedback and control. In practice, if you need precise position and torque holding you should use a standard servo or a motor with a suitable encoder and a closed-loop controller. If you need smooth continuous motion and simpler control, a continuous-rotation servo is an excellent lightweight choice.

keyIdea.title: Servo types
keyIdea.text: Standard servos for positional control, continuous-rotation servos for wheel-like motion; they interpret control signals differently.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Standard vs continuous-rotation servos
Standard servo
Moves to and holds a specific angle between its mechanical limits. Use when you need accurate positioning and holding torque.
Use case
Pan-tilt camera or robotic arm joint.
Control
Signal maps to angle; servo holds position.
Continuous-rotation servo
Rotates continuously; control input changes speed and direction rather than angle. Use for small-drive wheels and robots.
Use case
Drive wheels at variable speed without separate motor controller.
Control
Signal maps to speed/direction; cannot reliably hold a fixed angle.
Practical note
If you need both continuous motion and precise stopping, combine a continuous motor with an encoder and a control loop, or use a standard servo if holding position is primary.

screens.title: DC motors and why drivers are needed
screens.subtitle: DC motors draw more current than GPIO pins can supply and need a driver module

narration.text: DC motors provide continuous rotation and typically draw significantly more current than a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin can supply. Because of that, you must not connect a DC motor directly to a GPIO pin. A motor driver module such as the L298N or L293D sits between the Pi and the motor and provides the higher current paths as well as direction control through logic inputs. Motor drivers also let you control speed by accepting PWM for the enable or speed input. The gpiozero Motor class offers a simple software interface where you specify forward and backward GPIO pins and request forward, backward, stop, and a speed parameter for PWM-based speed control. From a wiring perspective, the motor driver has a separate motor power input which must be powered from an appropriate supply, and you should tie the driver ground to the Pi ground so logic signals reference the same ground. A common misconception is that a small motor will draw little current; stall conditions can draw high current briefly, so always plan your supply and driver for the worst-case current. The motor driver protects the Pi from motor current and provides an interface for direction and PWM control.

keyIdea.title: Driver necessity
keyIdea.text: Use a motor driver to handle high motor currents, provide direction logic, and accept PWM for speed; never power a DC motor directly from a GPIO.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › DC motors and why drivers are needed
Why a driver?
A motor driver provides higher current paths, direction logic, and accepts PWM for speed. It prevents high motor currents from flowing through Raspberry Pi pins.
Driver inputs
Logic pins from the Pi control direction and enable lines. PWM on the speed input controls motor velocity.
Motor power
Motor power comes from an external supply connected to the driver’s motor V+ terminal; size the supply for stall and continuous current.
Concrete example
Using an L298N: connect Pi GPIOs to the driver logic inputs, motor supply to the L298N VCC, tie the grounds, and use the enable pin with PWM to adjust speed. Then test forward and backward directions at low speed first.
Misconception to avoid
A small DC motor connected briefly might appear fine but can draw high current when stalled. Size the driver and power supply for peak draws and test under load cautiously.

screens.title: Motor driver modules and wiring patterns
screens.subtitle: How to connect logic, motor supply, and ground for reliable control

narration.text: A motor driver module sits between the Raspberry Pi and the DC motor. It has three distinct domains: logic inputs from the Pi, motor power inputs that supply the motor current, and the motor outputs that connect to the motor terminals. The correct wiring pattern is to power the motor supply separately with a voltage that matches the motor rating, connect the motor supply ground and the Pi ground together so the logic signals share a reference, and wire the Pi GPIO pins to the driver’s logic inputs for direction and enable. If the driver has an enable pin for speed, feed PWM from the Pi to that input. One practical wiring checklist is: 1) power off both supplies, 2) connect motor supply to driver motor V+, 3) connect driver ground and Pi ground, 4) connect direction pins to GPIO, 5) connect enable to PWM-capable GPIO, 6) power logic and then motor supply and test at low speed. A common mistake is forgetting the shared ground which makes the driver ignore or misinterpret logic signals. Another hazard is loose terminal screws that cause intermittent current spikes; always secure terminals and verify with small test runs before full-load operation.

keyIdea.title: Wiring architecture
keyIdea.text: Separate motor power and logic power, tie grounds, wire direction and PWM inputs, and follow a power-up checklist to avoid misinterpreted signals or damage.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Motor driver modules and wiring patterns
Driver domains
  • Logic inputs: GPIO pins that set direction and enable.
  • Motor power: separate V+ that supplies motor current.
  • Motor outputs: the terminals that feed the motor coils.
Power-up checklist
Power off → wire motor supply → tie grounds → attach GPIOs → power logic then motor → test at low speed.
Common mistakes and fixes
Missing common ground
Fix: Tie driver ground and Pi ground to ensure logic signals reference the same 0V.
Loose power terminals
Fix: Secure screws and test connections under low load before full operation.
Incorrect PWM pin
Fix: Use a PWM-capable GPIO for speed control and verify gpiozero accepts that pin for PWM output.

screens.title: External power requirements and common ground
screens.subtitle: Why motors need separate supplies and how to share ground correctly

narration.text: Motors and many actuators demand power levels beyond what the Raspberry Pi can provide. The correct approach is to use an external power supply sized for the motor's voltage and expected current, and then tie the motor supply ground to the Pi ground. This shared ground establishes a common reference so the Pi's logic signals have meaning to the driver or servo. A practical wiring sequence is: first, choose a motor supply with adequate voltage and current; second, connect the motor supply negative to the driver ground and the Pi ground; third, connect the motor positive to the driver's motor V+; fourth, connect logic pins from the Pi to the driver; and finally, power the motor supply after confirming the logic wiring. Always measure or estimate stall current and allow headroom when selecting the supply. A misconception is that matching voltage alone is sufficient; current capacity and transient spikes matter as much as steady voltage. Use decoupling capacitors on the motor supply and secure connections to reduce noise and voltage dips. These steps dramatically reduce the chance of the Pi resetting or signals becoming unreliable when the motor runs under load.

keyIdea.title: Power planning
keyIdea.text: Use an external supply sized for voltage and current, tie grounds to the Pi, and secure connections and decoupling to avoid noise and resets.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › External power requirements and common ground
Step-by-step power plan
  1. Estimate motor stall and continuous current and select a supply with margin.
  2. Connect motor supply negative to driver ground and Pi ground.
  3. Connect motor supply positive to the driver V+ terminal.
  4. Attach logic pins from Pi to driver, then power the logic and motor supplies in order.
Noise and stability tips
Add decoupling capacitors across motor power to smooth spikes and reduce electrical noise. Secure connections and avoid long thin wires for high-current paths to reduce voltage drops.
Warning

Never connect motor positive directly to Pi power rails if the motor draws significant current; this risks damaging the board and causing instability.

screens.title: Driving a DC motor with gpiozero Motor
screens.subtitle: A simple example shows forward, speed control, and stop

narration.text: The gpiozero library includes a Motor class that simplifies DC motor control when you connect a motor driver. To use it you create a Motor object specifying the forward and backward GPIO pins connected to the driver’s logic inputs. The Motor class provides methods such as forward, backward, and stop, and you can pass a speed parameter between 0 and 1 to control PWM-based speed. The example code in the visual demonstrates constructing a Motor bound to two GPIO pins, running forward at half speed for two seconds, then stopping. In practice, you connect the driver's enable or PWM pin to a PWM-capable GPIO and ensure the driver and motor receive the external motor supply. A typical misconception is thinking speed is controlled only by voltage; when using a driver you control speed by changing PWM duty cycle while keeping the motor supply voltage constant. Start with low speeds and short durations to confirm wiring and power stability, and watch for signs of voltage sag or heating. After testing, increase speed gradually until you meet your design needs while monitoring the motor and driver temperature.

keyIdea.title: Motor API
keyIdea.text: Use gpiozero's Motor(forward, backward) and call forward(speed=...), backward(speed=...), and stop() while powering the motor via a driver.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Driving a DC motor with gpiozero Motor
Code example
from gpiozero import Motor
from time import sleep

motor = Motor(forward=17, backward=18)

motor.forward(speed=0.5)
sleep(2)
motor.stop()
This uses two GPIOs for direction and PWM for speed. The actual motor current flows through the driver, not the Pi.
Practical notes
  • Bind forward/backward to driver logic pins, and use a PWM-capable GPIO for the enable line if required.
  • Start at low speed to confirm wiring and power stability before raising the duty cycle.
  • Monitor motor and driver temperature during extended runs and verify the power supply handles peaks.
Key Takeaway

Control speed with PWM through the driver; the Pi sends logic only. Never route motor current through GPIO pins.

screens.title: Relay modules and safe switching
screens.subtitle: How relays let the Pi control high-voltage loads and important safety steps

narration.text: A relay is an electrically operated switch that lets a low-voltage control signal operate a separate higher-voltage circuit. Relay modules designed for microcontrollers often include protection components like optocouplers and flyback diodes to reduce noise and protect the Pi from transients. Controlling a relay from gpiozero is simple: treat it like an output device and switch it on and off. However, the safety aspect is critical: when switching mains or high-power loads you must be trained to work with mains voltage, ensure secure insulated connections, use enclosures or terminal blocks, and double-check wiring before applying power. For low-voltage tests, toggle a small lamp or a bench power supply to confirm switching behavior. A common misconception is that a relay isolates all hazards — relays switch the load but the switched circuit still carries dangerous voltages that must be treated with the same respect as any mains wiring. In practice, use proper wire gauges, fuses, and secure terminals, and keep exposed conductors away from accidental contact. The simplest software example uses gpiozero’s OutputDevice to flip the relay and observe the click or state change, but always pair that with a strict hardware safety checklist before switching anything hazardous.

keyIdea.title: Relay safety
keyIdea.text: Relays enable switching of separate power circuits from the Pi, but wiring and hardware safety must be followed carefully when switching mains or high-power devices.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Relay modules and safe switching
How a relay works
A low-voltage signal energizes a coil or optocoupler to change the relay contacts and connect or disconnect the external circuit. The Pi controls the coil via a driver or module input.
Module features
Look for optocouplers and flyback diodes on microcontroller modules to protect the Pi from spikes.
Safe-practice checklist
  • Only work on mains wiring if trained and de-energized.
  • Secure terminals, use proper insulation, and mount the relay in an enclosure.
  • Test switching with low-voltage loads before applying mains.
Safety reminder
Relays switch the circuit but do not remove the hazard of the switched voltage. Treat switched circuits with full electrical safety practices.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three summary cards to keep in mind

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind as you build with actuators. First, servos are for positional control using PWM and a three-wire interface; use gpiozero's Servo class to move to min, mid, and max and always test with pauses. Second, DC motors require a motor driver and an external power supply; tie grounds between the Pi and the driver and control speed with PWM through the driver using gpiozero's Motor class. Third, relays let the Pi switch separate higher-voltage circuits but demand strict safety: secure terminals, proper insulation, and training for mains work. These points form the foundation of safe actuator design: choose the right actuator type, supply it with proper power through the correct interface hardware, and verify wiring before applying energy. Keep these concepts visible as you test and iterate your projects so you protect your Raspberry Pi and yourself while achieving reliable motion and switching.

keyIdea.title: Three core ideas
keyIdea.text: Servos for angle; drivers and external power for DC motors; relays for safe switching — always tie grounds and verify wiring.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts
Servo: precise angle
Use PWM and gpiozero's Servo methods to move and test min, mid, max positions.
DC motor: use a driver
Drivers handle motor current and direction; control speed with PWM and share ground with the Pi.
Relay: safe switching
Relays let you control separate high-voltage circuits. Follow full electrical safety practices when switching mains.
One-sentence summary

Choose the right actuator, use the correct interface and power, tie grounds, and always verify wiring for safe and reliable motion.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three concise cards you can recall while wiring or coding

narration.text: Here are three quick reference reminders you can use at the bench. First, never expect a GPIO pin to power a motor; always use a driver and external supply sized for the motor. Second, tie grounds between the Pi and the motor or driver so logic signals reference the same zero volt. Third, treat relays as a switch for a separate circuit and apply mains safety practices before switching any dangerous voltages. Keep these short rules in mind while you test servo sweeps, run motor speed trials, or toggle a relay; they will help you avoid common failures and protect your hardware. As you practice, make a short checklist for power-up and testing steps so each trial is safe and repeatable. That checklist is one of the best habits you can adopt as you build actuator-driven projects.

keyIdea.title: Bench reminders
keyIdea.text: GPIOs are for logic, grounds must be shared, and relays require safe handling — keep a power-up checklist at the bench.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts — Quick Reference
Power
Use an external supply sized for the motor's current.
Ground
Tie driver and Pi grounds so signals have the right reference.
Safety
Treat relays and switched circuits with full electrical precautions.
Final thought

A short bench checklist and cautious testing will keep your Pi and circuits safe while you learn to control the physical world.
